inventory.interpretation_note: The raw archive is much larger than the human interpretation surface. The dashboard should therefore show only the comparisons that answer a question cleanly, while the tables and files remain available for audit.

reading_guide.title: Comparability first
reading_guide.body: Direct clean rows, posterior framework rows, posterior decision rules, hybrid initializers, and active-sequential rows are not one pooled leaderboard. Each chart states its own comparison class.

reading_guide.title: Performance versus speedup
reading_guide.body: Performance improvements refer to elapsed time, train time, startup cost, and completed-run throughput. Speedup refers to a ratio against a baseline. The dashboard keeps those quantities separate.

reading_guide.title: Primary versus supporting evidence
reading_guide.body: The Hodgkin-Huxley fixed-task comparison is the empirical center. Benchmark parity, execution studies, and execution-path optimizations support or bound that comparison, but they do not replace it.

threads.title: Benchmark Parity and Split Integrity
threads.intro: These studies checked whether the inherited FitzHugh-Nagumo baseline remained statistically stable, and whether the archived split behavior remained scientifically interpretable.
threads.how_to_read: Read the metric-delta chart as a bounded difference against the archived benchmark mean, then read the ANOVA chart as a check that node count did not materially change predictive quality.
threads.main_conclusion: The baseline remained statistically close to the archived benchmark, while runtime changed more than predictive quality. The split issue mattered for interpretation, not for the later Hodgkin-Huxley frontier itself.

charts.title: Benchmark deltas against the archived FitzHugh-Nagumo reference
charts.subtitle: Positive values indicate the multi-seed rerun mean was above the archived benchmark value.
notes: The MSE offset is real, but it remains inside the reproduced multi-seed variation envelope.
The R2 shift is very small, which is why the parity conclusion remained positive.

charts.title: Node-count effect test on parity metrics
charts.subtitle: Higher p-values indicate weaker evidence that node count changed model quality.
notes: These p-values support the claim that the benchmark parity result is stable across the tested node counts.
The benchmark study therefore supports later systems claims without becoming a main objective.

threads.title: Execution Configuration and Run Policy
threads.intro: These studies determined which execution setting best supports broad comparative sweeps, while keeping the task fixed.
threads.how_to_read: The throughput chart answers the operational default question. The train-time chart answers a narrower question, namely whether tuned 2-node and 4-node lanes improved inside their own lane, which is different from asking whether multi-node scaling beat the best single-node policy.
threads.main_conclusion: Throughput-first grouped single-node execution became the practical default. Tuned 2-node and 4-node paths improved their own lane materially, but they did not overturn the broad-sweep single-node policy.

charts.title: Completed runs per hour, grouped 1-node versus selected 4-node latency path
charts.subtitle: Higher is better. The current Hodgkin-Huxley workload used the right-hand comparison.
notes: On the current Hodgkin-Huxley task, grouped single-node execution improved completed-run throughput by 85.5%.
This chart is why single-node remained the broad default even though 4-node latency could still be useful for targeted reference runs.

charts.title: Train-time reduction inside the tuned multi-node lane
charts.subtitle: These percentages compare the tuned `R1_accum2_nosync` lane against the earlier node-matched baseline.
notes: These are node-local improvements, not broad run-policy wins.
This is why performance and speedup should not be conflated in the dashboard text.

charts.title: Final grouped single-node factorization improvement
charts.subtitle: The `factor_s5` path was the last single-node cleanup before the broad default was closed.
notes: This was a small but clean single-node improvement that preserved quality.
Once this path existed, the case for broad 4-node default promotion became even weaker.

threads.title: Primary Direct Fixed-Task Comparison
threads.intro: This is the empirical center of the work. The current clean direct frontier is taken from the homogeneous A30 rerun package, which displaced the older mixed closure endpoint.
threads.how_to_read: Read the accuracy chart as the clean direct comparison within the direct-estimation class, and read the runtime chart separately, because runtime and accuracy are different objectives.
threads.main_conclusion: The direct clean winner is tuned Extra Trees, the robust direct representative is tuned k-nearest neighbors, and the best surviving neural direct row is materially behind both.

charts.title: Clean direct MAE by family representative
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. These rows share one direct-estimation comparison class.
notes: The clean gap from the best neural direct row to the direct winner is 43.1% on MAE.
The clean gap between the direct winner and the robust kNN representative is only 0.34%.

charts.title: Representative runtime by direct family
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. Runtime is not a quality metric, so it should be read separately from MAE.
notes: The direct clean winner was also much cheaper than the best surviving neural row.
The kNN representative remained the lowest-runtime direct contender while preserving near-winner clean accuracy.

threads.title: Posterior-Oriented and Representation Follow-Up
threads.intro: These studies broadened the state-of-the-art comparison through richer observations, stronger posterior families, and later aligned framework rows.
threads.how_to_read: The posterior chart is internal to the posterior-oriented family space. It should not be merged numerically with the direct clean frontier. The gain chart shows which interventions actually moved the posterior-oriented needle.
threads.main_conclusion: Observation enrichment improved SNPE materially, FMPE became the strongest clean posterior family in the checkpoint-2 block, and later BayesFlow decision rules improved MAE inside the aligned posterior branch without overturning the direct clean winner.

charts.title: Posterior-oriented clean MAE by representative
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. These rows remain inside the posterior-oriented result space.
notes: The BayesFlow median row is the best comparable posterior decision rule by MAE.
FMPE is still the clean posterior-family winner in the checkpoint-2 SBI block.
NPSE stayed slower and weaker than FMPE on the primary point metrics.

charts.title: Posterior-oriented intervention gains
charts.subtitle: Positive values are improvements against the reference named in each label. The combined-corruption row is intentionally negative.
categories: BayesFlow median versus framework MAE gain
notes: The richer observation space mattered before later family expansion.
The combined-corruption negative bar is a guardrail, because that branch damaged clean behavior too severely to promote.

charts.title: Posterior-oriented runtime by representative
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. This is performance, not quality.
notes: BayesFlow meanstd is the fastest aligned framework row among the promoted posterior-oriented representatives.
The MAE-optimal posterior decision rule is much slower than the aligned framework row, which is why the dashboard keeps accuracy and runtime in separate charts.

threads.title: Shift Robustness and Noise Sensitivity
threads.intro: These studies asked whether the clean winners survived perturbations, and whether shift-specific retraining changed the representative set.
threads.how_to_read: The first chart shows the clean-to-shift-specific posterior interventions. The second chart shows where the robust direct representative gains its practical value.
threads.main_conclusion: Robustness is plural. Matched drift and matched masking repairs are genuinely useful, while the robust direct representative is kNN rather than the clean tuned tree under additive noise.

charts.title: Shift-specific posterior improvement relative to the clean-trained feature-aware SNPE reference
charts.subtitle: Positive values indicate MAE improvement. The combined-corruption row shows why a single universal corruption-aware model was not promoted.
notes: The positive bars justify shift-specific promoted robustness paths.
The negative combined-corruption bar shows why one pooled robust-SNPE winner would have been misleading.

charts.title: kNN MAE improvement over the tuned tree under additive noise
charts.subtitle: Positive values indicate that kNN reduced MAE relative to `extra_trees_500_depth20` at that noise level.
notes: The direct clean winner and the direct robust winner are different, which is why the dashboard keeps them separate at the top.
The improvement stays material even at the heaviest tested additive noise level.

threads.title: Later Executable Extensions
threads.intro: These studies reduced missed-family risk through aligned framework runs, posterior decision rules, active-sequential ladders, and hybrid initializer rows.
threads.how_to_read: These charts are internal to their own extension class. They broaden coverage, but they do not replace the direct fixed-task comparison.
threads.main_conclusion: The best active-sequential row remained a simple Wasserstein smoke heuristic, ASNPE-style extension improved its own lane at a large runtime cost, and hybrid-initializer rows broadened coverage without entering the direct clean leaderboard.

charts.title: Active-sequential error metric by representative policy
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. This chart stays inside the active-sequential class.
notes: The simple Wasserstein smoke policy remained the best row in this class on the reported error metric.
ASNPE extended improved over earlier ASNPE ladders, but it did not become the best active-sequential representative overall.

charts.title: Active-sequential runtime by representative policy
charts.subtitle: Lower is better. The runtime gap is part of why these rows stayed in their own extension section.
notes: The later active ladder widened coverage dramatically, but the best class-level row was still the cheap Wasserstein heuristic.
This is one reason the extension studies should be read as coverage-expansion evidence rather than as a replacement leaderboard.

threads.title: Execution-Path Optimizations
threads.intro: These studies optimized startup behavior inside the extracted-data HH execution path. They mattered operationally, but they did not change the scientific frontier.
threads.how_to_read: The cache charts show startup reduction inside the execution path, not a change in model ranking. The explanation card below states why this branch was not expanded into a larger scientific campaign, even though the later mmap-backed canaries were strong.
threads.main_conclusion: Feature-scale caching reduced preprocessing materially, the mmap-backed split-array cache removed almost all startup overhead in the successful canaries, and the branch was tested far enough to prove viability, but it was not expanded into a large matrix because the main run-policy question had already closed on grouped single-node throughput.

charts.title: Feature-scale cache preprocessing reduction
charts.subtitle: Positive values indicate preprocessing time reduction relative to the eager path.
notes: This optimization attacked a measured startup bottleneck while preserving the eager hot loop.
That is why feature-scale cache became the extracted-data default before the split-array branch did.

charts.title: Split-array mmap startup reduction after the proof chain
charts.subtitle: Positive values indicate data-load reduction against the completed R4 medians for the same families.
notes: The first split-array canary failed badly, which is why the branch was initially kept experimental.

After the mmap-backed reload fix, the branch cleared both the dedicated launcher proof and a broader ordinary-launcher proof, so the question stopped being correctness and became one of marginal value.

cards.title: Why it was not tested as a full campaign
cards.body: The branch ultimately addressed startup overhead inside one extracted-data execution path. By the time the later proofs succeeded, the main systems question had already been answered by the throughput-first single-node policy, and the model-frontier question had already moved into family comparison, representation, and robustness work. So the split-array branch was tested enough to establish viability, while a full factorial expansion would have consumed effort without changing the main scientific claims.

cards.title: What was actually proved
cards.body: The later proof chain established that the split-array cache could be prewarmed, launched through its ordinary canary package, and then exercised through an older ordinary HH launcher once safe dataloader overrides were materialized automatically. That was enough for operational viability, even though it did not justify a new large experimental campaign.
